---
title: "For instructors"
---

This page is for whoever runs the course next: the author, a colleague, or
someone at another school. It holds the parts of the design that students do
not need to read: the module catalog and its variants, the session structure,
how to run the [learning journal](../course/learning-journal.qmd), how to ask a
guest to speak, and how to adapt the course for another cohort. The design
files themselves are in `curriculum/` in the
[repository](https://github.com/seandavi/ai-in-medicine-curriculum)
(private for now; it will be made public).

## The modules

Modules are independent. Each is one Zoom session, tags the competencies it
serves (`AIM-1` through `AIM-9` and `AIM-X`, defined in
`curriculum/competencies.md`), and assumes no prior module. That is what makes
the course survivable when a third of the class misses week two.

| ID | Chapter | Minutes | Competencies |
|---|---|---|---|
| `core-foundations` | [How these systems work](../chapters/core-foundations.qmd) | 75 | AIM-1, AIM-2 |
| `core-centaur-cyborg` | [Centaur or cyborg](../chapters/core-centaur-cyborg.qmd) | 90 | AIM-5, AIM-X, AIM-4 |
| `core-appraisal` | [Critical appraisal](../chapters/core-appraisal.qmd) | 90 | AIM-2, AIM-1, AIM-4, AIM-9 |
| `core-bias-equity` | [Bias and equity](../chapters/core-bias-equity.qmd) | 90 | AIM-3 |
| `core-patient-communication` | [Talking to patients about AI](../chapters/core-patient-communication.qmd) | 90 | AIM-6, AIM-4 |
| `core-ethics-regulation` | [Ethics, liability, and the device line](../chapters/core-ethics-regulation.qmd) | 75 | AIM-4, AIM-X |

Eleven modules, eight slots. The surplus is deliberate. Swap by cohort interest.

### The default assembly (fall 2026)

Since October 2026 the chapters are a framework and a menu, not a sequence to
teach. Each week has one **core** chapter and a menu of others. In weeks 2 to
4 the instructor's two weekly talks are the main event: Monday on the core
chapter's topic, Wednesday on a menu chapter or a topic beyond the book. The
core chapter is the companion to Monday's talk, read after it, or instead of
it by a student who missed it. Students spend most of their own time on
[Learn it with AI](../course/learn-with-ai.qmd).

| Week | Core (Monday talk) | Wednesday talk (class vote) | Menu |
|---|---|---|---|
| 1 | Centaur or cyborg | Week 1 is taught live; no vote | How these systems work (covered by the live talks) |
| 2 | Prompting lab | Scholarly writing, or answers grounded in real sources | Critical appraisal; Bias and equity; Grounding AI in real sources |
| 3 | Talking to patients about AI | Bias and equity, or building a small tool live | Agentic coding; the scribe open lab |
| 4 | Ethics, liability, and the device line | Where this is going (jobs, the planet) and what you will keep; no vote | Will AI take your job?; What AI costs the planet |

: Core chapter, Wednesday talk, and menu by week. Wednesday topics are a starting plan for fall 2026. {#tbl-default}

Coverage check: the core chapters make AIM-2, AIM-4, AIM-5, and AIM-6 main
subjects. AIM-1 is covered by the week 1 live talks. **AIM-3 (bias) is not in a
core chapter**; it is covered by the week 2 Friday scenario card on bias, by
the bias chapter on the menu, and by the week 3 Wednesday talk if the class
votes for it. This is a deliberate trade, recorded in
`curriculum/design-constraints.md`.

### Variants

**A cohort that wants more evidence and appraisal.** Make critical appraisal the
week 2 core and the prompting lab a menu item.

**A cohort with no live week 1.** Make How these systems work the week 1 core.

### Three ideas that recur

Modules are independent, but three ideas recur across all of them. Name them in
week one and call them by name whenever they reappear. They are what turns
eight sessions into a course, and they are what students will still have when
every tool taught here has been replaced.

1. **Proxies fail.** Almost every AI failure in medicine is a stand-in that
   looked reasonable. Cost stood in for need in the Obermeyer algorithm. Light
   skin stood in for normal reflectance in pulse oximetry. Race stood in for
   unmeasured biology in eGFR. A benchmark score stood in for clinical
   performance in FDA clearance data. The question to train is always: *what is
   this actually measuring, and what was it substituted for?*
2. **Efficiency gains get eaten by volume.** Per-unit improvement is
   cancelled out by growth in use, and this appears in three separate literatures.
   Google cut per-prompt energy while total emissions rose. AI made
   radiologists more productive and imaging demand grew faster. AI scribes cut
   documentation time per note, and the time went into seeing more patients.
   Efficiency is not the same as less.
3. **The published number is the optimistic one.** Before-and-after pilots on
   self-selected early adopters beat randomized trials. Vendor benchmarks on
   curated hard cases beat real-world deployment. The gap between the most
   prominently reported statistic and the trial result is the most reliable
   teaching material in this field.

## Running a week

Weeks 2 to 4 have the same shape, so students always know what comes next.
Week 1 is taught live on its own schedule (see the
[syllabus](../course/syllabus.qmd)).

| When | What |
|---|---|
| Monday, 60 min, live and recorded | Opens with 20 to 30 minutes of **"How I used AI this week"**: the instructor's own real, unpolished tasks, talked through on screen, including one that went wrong and how it was caught. End that part with a dare: try one of these this week. No patient data or confidential review material on screen. Then a talk on the week's core chapter topic, with live demonstrations. |
| Wednesday, 60 min, live and recorded | A talk on a menu chapter or a topic beyond the book. The class votes the week before from a short list. |
| On their own | The core chapter, after Monday's talk or instead of it (about 1 hour), and [Learn it with AI](../course/learn-with-ai.qmd) (2 to 4 hours). Menu chapters and [open labs](open-labs.qmd) are optional. |
| Through the week | Guest talks; students attend or watch one. |
| Thursday, 45 min, live | Office hours: students bring what they are stuck on. Not recorded. [Learning journal](../course/learning-journal.qmd) entry due that night. |
| Friday, 60 min | Small group: what AI taught you, one thing you caught, then the [scenario cards](../course/friday-groups.qmd) practised out loud. |

: A week in the course, weeks 2 to 4. Recordings count as attending. {#tbl-week-run}

The instructor's cost is real: about 6.75 live hours a week (Monday, Wednesday,
Thursday, and four Friday slots) plus two new talks to write. An instructor
with less time can run the Wednesday talk as an open lab or hand it to a
guest.

Running notes:

- **Lead with use, not warnings.** Students' feedback in earlier years was that
  they were afraid to use chatbots. The safety rules are short and stated once;
  checking is taught as part of using the tool well, not as a reason to avoid it.
- **Everything uses synthetic data.** No real patient information in any course
  activity, in any account.
- **Ungraded means every hour has to be worth it.** Each live session should
  leave students having done something, not only having heard something.

## Running the learning journal

The [student page](../course/learning-journal.qmd) has the four questions. Mark
each entry complete or incomplete. In weeks 1 and 2, reply with one sentence:
what to try next. Use Friday's small group, not written feedback, for anything
longer. Shared resources that are worth keeping go into the starter resources
appendix after a quick check.

The week 4 piece ("what you will keep") is presented in five minutes at the
last Friday group. That session is the course's close.

## Asking a guest to speak

The design caps guests deliberately: one per session, two across the whole
course. Every session pairs an idea with an activity, and a guest-heavy course
turns back into lectures without anyone deciding to.

The most useful guest is someone who can talk about a tool actually deployed in
the local health system in the last quarter. That is what a fourth-year
audience wants and what a survey lecture cannot give. Good matches by module:
ambient documentation as deployed (centaur or cyborg); disclosure
conversations and a patient-facing tipsheet (talking to patients); how a tool
gets approved and bought locally (appraisal); the device boundary and local
policy (ethics); a proxy failure in a model that was really deployed (bias and
equity); what AI is doing to one specialty's job market (workforce).

The invitation should say: the date and time; a twenty-minute slot inside a
ninety-minute session, never a fifty-minute lecture; the competency the
session serves; Zoom only; about forty fourth-year students; ungraded; and the
actual ask, *bring one thing you deployed and one thing that went wrong.*
Sending the invitations as one batch with a dean's co-signature gets
more acceptances. Sending them one at a time does not.

## Adapting the course for another cohort

Everything specific to the original offering (people, dates, local accounts)
is kept out of the chapters on purpose, so the book can be reassembled
elsewhere. To run it for your own cohort:

1. **Check the design constraints** in `curriculum/design-constraints.md`
   against yours. The chapters assume about forty fourth-year students, four
   weeks, Zoom, ungraded, and free tiers. If you have fewer weeks, use the
   one-session-a-week variant above.
2. **Choose an assembly.** The default or one of the variants. Update the
   [syllabus](../course/syllabus.qmd) tables and the due-date placeholders.
3. **Confirm tool access.** The chapters assume one general-purpose chatbot
   without a signup step. Several `[VERIFY]` flags in the chapters are access
   details to confirm the week before: an institutional NotebookLM login, a
   student plan's status, an episode still being online. The open flags are
   listed in one GitHub issue on the repository.
4. **Set your own institution's policy text** where a chapter says to check
   it, for example the attestation language for ambient documentation in
   centaur or cyborg, and your state's disclosure statutes in talking to
   patients.
5. **Choose your guests**, if any, using the section above.
6. **Write the exemplar week** of the resource log yourself. Students copy
   what they see.

Chapters are reviewed against six invented readers before they change; the
[Review personas](personas.qmd) appendix has them, and the
[How this book was made](about.qmd) appendix says how the review runs. If you
change a chapter, review it as the six.
